sm: Tim Rice opens the District Club by noting that after the midterms, leadership fights have broken out in both parties and both chambers. He is joined by Mary Margaret Olohan, Dylan Hausmann and guest Kate Andrews. The first topic is Susie Wiles leaving as White House chief of staff and Stephen Miller taking the job. Andrews says Miller dislikes profiles but speaks openly online, and that she would normally expect a doubling down on deportations. She points out, though, that Trump sounded softer on immigration in his 60 Minutes interview.

Olohan replies that the interview was recorded hours before Miller's elevation was announced, and says Miller will have far more sway than before. She cites his new memo barring unapproved contact between White House staff and lobbyists, a notable move since Wiles came from the lobbying world. Hausmann expects aggressive rhetoric but few policy levers, because Congress will not pass Trump's agenda and Democrats can threaten shutdowns. Andrews adds that Trump's concern for his legacy, on issues like AI and immigration, may pull against Miller, and that Democrats may not want to work with Trump anyway.

The panel turns to whether Democrats will cooperate with Trump on areas like drug prices. Hakeem Jeffries has said Democrats will not work with Miller or the president, which Rice compares to Mitch McConnell's approach. Andrews notes that incoming senators such as James Talarico have struck a more conciliatory tone, while she fears newly elected members will get caught up in infighting. Olohan expects investigations and vengeance, pointing to comments from some Democrats, while Hausmann notes Democrats are divided between those wanting oversight and those wanting to pursue progressive policy.

The discussion focuses on Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed and his idea of a Trump-branded Medicare for All card. Olohan thinks he mostly wants attention and is beholden to the radical left, while Andrews and Hausmann argue he is an ideological purist and a leader of that wing. They compare his approach to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's playbook of winning over Trump personally. Rice and Andrews suggest Trump's tariffs and government stakes in businesses have socialist tendencies.

Olohan argues Trump likes Mamdani as a person, not for his policies, and doubts the same warmth would extend to El Sayed given criticism of the vice president. The group then discusses the CBS interview in which Trump was asked whether he would forgive his enemies. Olohan found the question presumptuous, while Hausmann said Trump's ethic resembles Achilles more than Christ. Andrews liked it because viewers watched the president think in real time.

Rice moves to congressional Republicans, who have kept most of their leaders. Tom Emmer stays as whip, John Thune stays in the Senate, and Jim Jordan becomes House Minority Leader. Hausmann says Jordan will be effective, but the Thune situation matters more. He argues many moderate Republicans who once blocked Jordan lost their seats, so the conference is more hard-line. He thinks Jordan's real significance comes if Republicans retake the House and he moves toward the speakership.

The panel asks what Republicans wanted Thune to do differently, beyond passing the Save America Act by ending the filibuster. Olohan says she asked Trump last weekend about Thune. Trump called him a good man but said the choice is up to Republicans, which she reads as openness to a change. Hausmann thinks Trump would already have acted if he cared. Andrews says Thune's re-election by his senators shows they expected little different, and suggests the filibuster could become a Republican argument in 2028.

The group debates whether delaying the leadership elections would have mattered, and most think it would only have prolonged the fighting. Hausmann says it is odd to take such a beating and then return with the same plan. Olohan criticizes Thune and Mike Johnson for saying they could have done nothing differently and calls the lack of reflection disturbing. Andrews worries 2028 will become a Medicare for All campaign. Hausmann replies that tariffs, the Iran war, deportations and corruption drove the loss, though leaders should still take some responsibility.
sg: Stephen Miller Becomes Chief of Staff
